implementation_notes: Modern default: the entity is a POCO with no persistence members, and the mapping is declared separately in an IEntityTypeConfiguration<T> class (ToTable, HasKey, Property, HasConversion) applied through modelBuilder; DbSet<T> is the persistence facade. Entity Framework Core reads this model at startup, so the domain type stays free of schema vocabulary and attributes alike, and the same metadata feeds migrations and the compiled model. Data annotations remain a legitimate compact variant for small models.
pitfalls: A configuration class that is never discovered (assembly scan missing, wrong namespace) is a silent no-op: the mapping falls back to conventions.
Tracked instances may be proxies with change-tracking snapshots and lazy loading; the entity is persistence-ignorant but not proxy-ignorant.

variants.name: Data Annotations on the entity
variants.implementation_notes: Compact variant: [Table], [Key], [Column], [MaxLength] and [NotMapped] sit on the POCO itself; the entity still contains no persistence calls, but schema details now appear in the type declaration. Prefer it for small models; switch to fluent configuration when the mapping needs value converters, composite keys or per-environment differences.
pitfalls: When annotations and fluent configuration both exist, the fluent API wins - the effective mapping may not be what the class suggests.
Forgetting [NotMapped] on a computed property makes EF Core try to persist a column that does not exist.
